newsitem.title: CHILE: Escondida miners begin strike, says union.
newsitem.headline: Escondida miners begin strike, says union.

text.p: A small minority of workers at Chile's Escondida copper mine began an indefinite strike early Friday to demand wage increases, a union leader said.

About 120 workers at the mine near the northern city of Antofagasta went on strike as of the first morning shift at 0800 local/1300 GMT, said union official Pablo Godoy at union headquarters in Antofagasta.

Most of Escondida's roughly 300 unionized workers, out of a total workforce of 2,000, voted Wednesday to strike from Friday. They ratified the decision at an assembly Thursday night, and about 80 more workers were expected to join the strike when the next shift begins at 2000 local.
Escondida officials have said the strike's effect on production will be practically nil.

Still, the conflict is being closely watched by other Chilean mining companies because it could give a sign of union strength in the copper industry. State-owned Codelco's copper mines are all unionized but most of the region's private mines, many of which began operations only in the last few years, have only minority union representation or none at all.
The stakes are especially high at Escondida, the world's largest copper mine with annual production at over 800,000 tonnes. The mine is owned by Broken Hill Proprietary and RTZ Corp plc.

"This strike sets a precedent. The effect of it will be felt in future wage negotiations, not on production, because the effect on production is zero," said an Escondida official Thursday, asking not to be identified.
The striking workers are scattered throughout all of Escondida's operations, which include the open pit, concentrators, a cathodes plant and a port at Puerto Coloso near Antofagasta.
But the highest concentrations of unionized workers are in the mine itself and on machinery maintenance, said the Escondida official.
